question: Which risks are shared across all peer companies??
cypher:
MATCH (tc:TargetCompany)
OPTIONAL MATCH (peer:Company {is_peer:true})-[:COMPETES_WITH]->(tc)
OPTIONAL MATCH (peer)-[:FACES_RISK]->(r:Risk)
WITH tc, COLLECT(DISTINCT peer.name) AS peers, COLLECT(DISTINCT r.name) AS all_peer_risks
WITH tc, peers, all_peer_risks, SIZE(peers) AS total_peers
UNWIND all_peer_risks AS risk_name
WITH tc, total_peers, risk_name, COUNT(risk_name) AS risk_count
WHERE risk_count = total_peers
RETURN DISTINCT tc.name AS company, COLLECT(DISTINCT risk_name) AS shared_risks

risk.name: Change in control from issuance of additional shares
risk.description: Issuing a substantial number of additional shares could trigger a change in control, affecting NOL usage and management structure.
risk.why: A large issuance of Class A common stock could cause a change in control, potentially impacting the company’s ability to use net operating loss carryforwards and leading to officer/director changes.

risk.name: Lack of operating history impairs ability to evaluate business prospects
risk.description: As a blank check company with no operations, investors have no basis to assess ability to complete a business combination.
risk.why: The company has no operating results and will not generate revenue until completing an initial business combination, making it impossible to evaluate its performance or success prospects.

risk.name: Management may lack expertise to evaluate target businesses outside their area
risk.description: Pursuing a business combination outside management’s expertise may lead to inadequate risk assessment and reduced shareholder value.
risk.why: Management’s expertise may not apply to evaluating or operating a target outside their field, and they may fail to ascertain or assess all significant risk factors, potentially reducing share value.

risk.name: Risks from cross-border business combinations
risk.description: Pursuing a target outside the U.S. exposes the company to international risks including due diligence challenges, regulatory approvals, and currency fluctuations.
risk.why: Cross-border deals involve additional burdens like foreign due diligence, local government approvals, and exchange rate fluctuations that could affect transaction price or completion.

risk.name: Global climate change laws and regulations
risk.description: New or expanded GHG regulations could increase production costs, especially for energy use, and limit our ability to compete globally.
risk.why: Regulations like carbon pricing, emissions permits, or renewable targets may raise energy costs; we may be unable to pass these costs to customers, reducing liquidity and operating income.

risk.name: Inability to refinance debt or generate sufficient cash flow
risk.description: Insufficient operating cash flows may prevent timely debt repayment or refinancing, risking default or unfavorable terms.
risk.why: The company must pay $790M in total commitments in 2023, and future cash flows depend on factors beyond its control; refinancing may not be possible on favorable terms or at all.

risk.name: Regulatory restrictions on TiO2 use or increased compliance costs
risk.description: New environmental or health regulations may restrict TiO2 use, reduce demand, or increase manufacturing and compliance costs.
risk.why: Regulations in operating or selling countries could classify or limit TiO2 applications, affecting consumer perception and increasing compliance burdens that reduce sales or raise costs.

risk.name: Dilution or financial burden from raising capital
risk.description: Raising capital through equity or debt could dilute shareholders or divert cash flow to debt payments.
risk.why: Equity financing would dilute existing shareholders, while debt financing would dedicate significant operating cash flow to principal and interest payments, limiting funds for business activities.

risk.name: High speculative nature due to upfront capital needs
risk.description: Investment in the company is highly speculative due to substantial upfront capital expenditures and uncertainty of commercial viability.
risk.why: The company expects to incur operating losses and negative cash flows indefinitely while executing its business plan, with no assurance it will ever achieve profitability.

risk.name: Limitations on net operating loss (NOL) carryforwards
risk.description: The company’s ability to use its $1.321 trillion U.S. federal NOL carryforwards may be limited by tax law restrictions and ownership changes.
risk.why: NOLs from pre-2018 may expire unused; post-2017 NOLs are limited to 80% of taxable income, and an ownership change under Sections 382/383 could further restrict usage, increasing future tax liability.

risk.name: Regulatory compliance failures
risk.description: Failure to comply with federal, state, local, and non-U.S. regulations on building codes, safety, and hydrogen infrastructure may trigger sanctions.
risk.why: Government sanctions could materially adversely affect business, operating results, and financial condition, and responding to enforcement actions diverts management attention and increases professional fees.

risk.name: Risks from acquisitions and integrations
risk.description: Acquiring and integrating businesses or assets carries risks of failure to meet expectations, integration issues, or unanticipated liabilities.
risk.why: The company may not complete transactions on favorable terms, acquired assets may underperform, integration may fail, or hidden liabilities may emerge without adequate contractual protections or insurance.

risk.name: Short operating history and minimal revenue
risk.description: The company has a limited operating history and has generated minimal revenue, making it difficult to evaluate its prospects.
risk.why: Incorporated in August 2015, the company lacks sufficient historical data for investors to assess viability, increasing uncertainty about its success in a new industry with no established comparables.

Executive Summary

Worldwide sales decreased 2% in 2024 to $2.119 billion as compared with $2.170 billion in 2023. Consolidated income from operations was $286.5 million, as compared with $171.8 million in the prior year. Included in income from operations for 2024 was $11.3 million of litigation expenses incurred in connection with the bankruptcy of the Company’s subsidiaries, BMI Oldco Inc. (f/k/a Barretts Minerals Inc.) ("Oldco") and Barretts Ventures Texas LLC ("BVT" and together with Oldco, the "Chapter 11 Debtors"). In addition, in 2024, the Company entered into a Debtor-in-Possession Credit Agreement with Oldco (the "DIP Credit Agreement") which resulted in a $30.0 million provision for credit loss charge. The Company refinanced its senior secured revolving credit facility and term loan in the fourth quarter of 2024, increasing the aggregate commitments under the revolving credit facility to $400 million and extending out maturities to 2029 for the revolving credit facility and 2031 for the term loan. In connection with the refinancing, the Company incurred $1.8 million of debt extinguishment expenses.

In 2024, the Company continued to deliver on its strategic growth initiatives driven by multi-year advancements in new product development, positioning in growth markets and geographies, geographic penetration and growth from acquisitions.

The Company currently has more than $700 million of available liquidity, including cash on hand, as well as availability under its revolving credit facility. We believe these factors will allow us to meet our anticipated funding requirements. Our intention is to maintain a balanced approach to capital deployment, by using cash flow for investments in growth, returns to shareholders, and continued debt reduction.

Note 21. Segment and Related Information

The Company determines its operating segments based on the discrete financial information that is regularly evaluated by its chief operating decision maker, our Chief Executive Officer, in deciding how to allocate resources and in assessing performance. The Company’s operating segments are strategic business units that offer different products and serve different markets. They are managed separately and require different technology and marketing strategies.

The Company has

two

reportable segments: the Consumer & Specialties segment and the Engineered Solutions segment.

The Consumer & Specialties segment serves consumer end markets directly and provides mineral-based solutions and technologies that are essential to our customers’ products. The

two

product lines in this segment are Household & Personal Care - our mineral-to-shelf product line that serves pet care, personal and household care, fluid purification and other consumer oriented markets, and Specialty Additives, delivering specialty mineral additives to a variety of consumer and industrial end markets including paper, packaging, construction, automotive, and food and pharmaceuticals.

The Engineered Solutions segment combines all engineered systems, mineral blends, and technologies that are designed to aid in customer processes and projects. The

two

product lines in this segment are High-Temperature Technologies – combining all of our mineral-based blends, technologies, and systems serving the foundry, steel, glass, aluminum and other high-temperature processing industries, and Environmental & Infrastructure, which includes environmental and remediation solutions such as geosynthetic clay lining systems, water remediation technologies as well as drilling, commercial building and infrastructure-related products.

The accounting policies of the segments are the same as those described in the summary of significant accounting policies. The Company evaluates performance based on the operating income of the respective business units. The costs deducted to arrive at operating profit do not include several items, such as net interest or income tax expense. Depreciation expense related to corporate assets is allocated to the business segments and is included in their income from operations. The Company determines its operating segments based on the discrete financial information that is regularly evaluated by its chief operating decision maker, our Chief Executive Officer, in deciding how to allocate resources and in assessing performance.
